name: TOPLESS THE MORNING TO YOU BURGER

recipe.history:
The open-faced sandwich — a preparation in which the bottom half of a bread base supports a full array of toppings while the top is either absent or served alongside for assembly — has deep roots across multiple culinary traditions simultaneously. The Scandinavian smørrebrød, dating back at least to the fifteenth century, is perhaps the most refined expression of this form: dense rye bread spread with butter and piled with cured fish, pickled vegetables, soft cheeses, and sliced meats in elaborate compositions that were never meant to be closed. In the American context, the open-faced hot sandwich became a diner staple by the mid-twentieth century, with hot turkey sandwiches, beef and gravy combinations, and the classic patty melt all appearing in this approachable, unguarded format. The removal of the top bun is not laziness — it is an invitation to see and appreciate every element of a dish rather than obscuring it beneath a lid.

The open-faced burger as a deliberate culinary statement emerged alongside the artisan burger movement of the late 2000s and early 2010s, when chefs began reconsidering every assumption about what a burger needed to be. Without a top bun to compress and trap steam, the toppings on an open-faced burger remain distinct and individually articulated — each ingredient visible, textured, and tasted on its own terms rather than blurred together under pressure. This format also privileges the visual and demands that the cook take genuine care with arrangement, because there is nothing hidden. It is a more honest burger in that sense: the quality of your ingredients and your technique are completely exposed, which is either a vulnerability or a statement of confidence, depending on the cook.

I built my first intentional open-faced burger on a Tuesday morning when I had exactly one bun left and two people who wanted burgers. The decision was made by circumstance, but the result was its own kind of revelation. With the top off, I could pile the toppings freely — a runny fried egg, caramelized onions, sharp cheddar that draped over the sides of the patty, a sprig of fresh thyme, a bright streak of hot sauce — and the whole thing looked like a small still life. We ate them with knives and forks, which felt ceremonial in the best way, and the egg yolk ran down through everything and became a sauce all on its own. The topless burger, I realized, was simply a burger that had decided to be honest about what it was.

Medium rare, at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — is the only temperature at which a beef patty is fully itself. This is especially true in an open-faced preparation, where the patty is the unchallenged visual and structural centerpiece of the dish and must carry the full weight of the meal. A well-seared, medium-rare patty has a crust that crackles and gives way to a warm, rosy interior that is succulent in the truest sense — genuinely full of juice, full of fat, full of the deep mineral and umami notes that make beef worth eating. Overcooking diminishes all of this. It compresses the texture into something uniform, drives out the moisture, and flattens the flavor profile into a single grey note. At medium rare, every bite of the open-faced burger is a complete experience.
ingredients: For the open-faced assembly (bottom bun only):
1 brioche burger bun bottom half (top bun set aside or omitted)
A handful of baby arugula or watercress
1 large yellow onion, halved and thinly sliced
instructions: 1. Make the caramelized onions: melt butter with olive oil in a heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Add sliced onions and salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 30 to 40 minutes until deeply golden and sweet. Stir in balsamic vinegar and cook 1 minute more. Set aside.
2. Cook the bacon in a skillet over medium heat until crispy, about 4 to 5 minutes per side. Drain on paper towels and set aside.

3. Remove the ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking. Form gently into a single patty about 4 inches in diameter and 3/4-inch thick. Press a dimple in the center with your thumb. Season both sides with kosher salt, black pepper, and smoked paprika.
4. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add neutral oil and swirl to coat.
5. Place the patty in the pan and cook undisturbed for 3 minutes to build a deep crust.
6. Flip once. Lay cheddar slices over the patty immediately. Cook 2 to 3 more minutes.
7. Check internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer. Remove at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Tent loosely with foil and rest 3 minutes.

8. While the patty rests, melt butter in a separate small non-stick pan over medium heat. Crack the egg in and fry sunny-side up until whites are set but yolk is still fully runny, about 2 to 3 minutes. Season with a pinch of salt.
9. Toast the brioche bun bottom cut-side up under the broiler or in a buttered pan until golden, 1 to 2 minutes. Leave the top bun off — this is an open-faced burger.
10. Spread mayonnaise and whole grain mustard on the toasted bun bottom.

11. Layer in order: arugula or watercress, tomato slices, the medium-rare patty with melted cheddar, caramelized onions, bacon strips crossed over the top, and the fried egg placed last so the yolk is the crown of the dish.
12. Drizzle hot sauce over the egg and toppings.
13. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and a scattering of fresh thyme leaves.
14. Serve immediately on a plate with a knife and fork — this burger is meant to be eaten open-faced, not folded or closed.
